# Surface model

Surfaces are the system's spatial grammar. They decide what feels like the page, what feels like a contained object, and what feels temporarily elevated above the rest of the interface.

The shipped model separates static `surface` treatment from floating `overlay` treatment. Static recipes currently receive a low-lift default shadow; overlays receive a stronger elevation. The design rule is still restrained: use borders and contrast first, and reserve stronger shadows for spatially elevated UI.

## Why this exists

Without a surface model, every component invents its own depth:

- cards get shadows because they look "nice";
- inputs get inner shadows that fight borders;
- dropdowns and dialogs use the same treatment as static panels;
- dark mode turns into a stack of similar gray rectangles.

The goal is to make depth meaningful. A user should be able to infer interaction from the surface treatment before reading any text.

## Surface roles

| Role | Canonical token | Tailwind/shadcn adapter | Typical use |
|------|-----------------|-------------------------|-------------|
| Page | `--a63-surface-page` | `background` | Routes, full-page layouts |
| Object | `--a63-surface-panel` | `card` | Cards, panels, list sections |
| Muted | `--a63-surface-muted` | `muted` | Toolbars, inactive rows, subtle fills |
| Floating | `--a63-surface-overlay` | `popover` | Menus, popovers, dialogs |
| Input | `--a63-surface-control` | recipe-owned (`input` is the border role) | Inputs, selects, textareas |
| Border | `--a63-border-subtle` / `--a63-border-control` | `border` / `input` | Cards, fields, dividers |

The tokens matter because they let components share intent. A dialog and a dropdown both use `--a63-surface-overlay` because they are temporary layers. A static settings panel should use `--a63-surface-panel`, even if it visually resembles one.

## Elevation rules

| Surface | Border | Shadow | Reason |
|---------|--------|--------|--------|
| Page canvas | No | No | It is the base layer |
| Static card | Usually yes | Low lift in the shipped surface contract | It groups content without competing with overlays |
| Input or trigger | Yes | No | The control is interactive, not elevated |
| Popover / menu | Yes | Yes, subtle | It floats above the page |
| Dialog / sheet | Yes | Yes | It interrupts the current layer |
| OS window | Yes | Yes | It models an independent spatial object |

Control-family shadows are separate from overlay elevation. A theme may give buttons a bevel or fields an inset, but controls still use state tokens rather than adopting the overlay shadow.

## Theming the treatment: surface & overlay contracts

The roles and elevation rules above describe the *default* look. Themes then reskin the **treatment** of a surface — its glass, bevel, phosphor, texture — without changing the contract's semantic role. A theme may separately remap semantic paint; color does not travel through these treatment handles. That variation runs through two contracts, mirroring the control contract:

- **`surface`** — the static, in-flow container (cards, panels, frames, sections, the attached-tabs body).
- **`overlay`** — the floating, elevated surface (popovers, menus, selects, tooltips, dialogs, sheets, drawers). Plus one overlay-only handle for drag elevation.

Color is **not** part of the contract. A surface's fill still reads `--a63-surface-panel` / `--a63-surface-overlay`, its border reads `--a63-border-subtle`, its text reads `--a63-text-*` — all semantic. The contract carries only the theme-varying *treatment*, exactly like the control contract exposes gloss and shadow but not the action color.

### The handle set

Both archetypes expose the same core vocabulary (`X` = `surface` | `overlay`) with different `:root` defaults — a static surface has low lift, while a floating one elevates. Overlay adds a drag-shadow handle.

| Handle | Purpose |
|--------|---------|
| `--a63-X-shadow` | Outer elevation — flush, bevel, drop, or glow |
| `--a63-X-inner-shadow` | Recessed/inset treatment (a sunken well) |
| `--a63-X-gloss` | Top-half sheen (a `background-image` gradient) — aqua glass |
| `--a63-X-highlight` (+ `-opacity`) | Rim/edge specular highlight |
| `--a63-X-backdrop` | `backdrop-filter` (blur/saturate) — glassy translucency |
| `--a63-X-border-style` + `--a63-X-border-width` | Bevel — outset/inset/solid, 1–2px |
| `--a63-X-texture-image` + `--a63-X-texture-blend` | A texture layer (scanline/pinstripe) and its blend mode |
| `--a63-X-radius` | Optional family override; shipped themes leave it unset so the radius axis and recipe fallback win |
| `--a63-overlay-drag-shadow` *(overlay only)* | Elevation while a floating surface is dragged (widgets, window frames) |

Widgets and window frames are compositions over the overlay archetype. Widgets also have a specialized `widget` contract that aliases overlay handles and adds rim/weather hooks; window frames consume overlay handles directly while their geometry lives in `@atom63/os63`.

### The three-layer flow

Treatment resolves the same way the control contract does:

1. **`:root` default** — surface and overlay shadows establish low and floating elevation. Gloss, highlight, backdrop, and texture default inert; borders default to `solid 1px`. Radius is deliberately *not* defaulted here.
2. **Theme override** — a theme sets handles under `[data-a63-theme='…']`: Aqua adds gloss, backdrop blur, and highlights; Retro uses outset 2px borders and bevel shadows; Terminal adds a scanline texture and phosphor edges. Corner shape stays on the independent radius axis.
3. **Recipe consumes** — a component reads the handles at its use-site, opting into as much or as little as it wants:

```css
background-image: var(--a63-surface-gloss), var(--a63-surface-texture-image);
background-blend-mode: normal, var(--a63-surface-texture-blend);
backdrop-filter: var(--a63-surface-backdrop);
box-shadow: var(--a63-surface-inner-shadow, none), var(--a63-surface-shadow);
border: var(--a63-surface-border-width) var(--a63-surface-border-style) var(--a63-border-subtle);
border-radius: var(--a63-surface-radius, var(--radius-3xl));
```

Once a recipe references the handles, every theme reskins it for free — no per-component theme CSS.

### Two rules that keep this safe

- **Radius has no `:root` default.** Surface recipes have divergent radii (a card is round, a tooltip is tight), so a single contract default would flatten them. Each recipe reads `var(--a63-X-radius, <its own radius>)`; shipped themes leave this override unset, and the independent radius axis changes the fallback scale.
- **The contract is additive.** Because every handle defaults to an inert value and every recipe reads it with a fallback to today's value, adding the contract changes nothing in the modern theme. A visible change in modern is a bug, not a feature. A surface that is glassy *by default* (a frosted control) keeps its literal `backdrop-filter` rather than consuming a handle that would default it away.

## State vs elevation

Do not use shadow as a generic interaction state.

| Need | Prefer | Avoid |
|------|--------|-------|
| Hover feedback | Background or border shift | New shadow |
| Pressed feedback | Motion, inset tone, `data-pressed` color | Drop shadow |
| Focus feedback | Focus ring | Shadow glow |
| Disabled state | Opacity and pointer behavior | Lowered shadow |
| Floating layer | Popover/dialog shadow | Flat border only |

State answers "what is happening to this control?" Elevation answers "where does this surface sit in space?" Mixing those two makes the interface harder to read.

## Dark mode

Dark mode changes the usefulness of shadows. On dark surfaces, shadows are less visible and often less useful. Border, contrast, and backdrop separation carry more of the work.

Use these cues in dark mode:

- border contrast for static separation;
- background contrast for nested surfaces;
- backdrop or overlay for modal focus;
- subtle shadow only when a surface truly floats.

## Decision rules

1. Start flat.
2. Add a border when content needs grouping.
3. Add background contrast when a nested surface needs its own identity.
4. Add shadow only when the object floats above the current layer.
5. Use motion and color for state feedback, not elevation.

## Anti-patterns

```tsx
// Avoid: every object asks for depth.
```

This makes static, editable, and floating elements compete for the same visual signal.

```tsx
// Prefer: depth follows spatial meaning.
```

The button and input remain controls. The card remains a static object. The popover is the thing that floats.

## Review checklist

When reviewing a new component, ask:

1. Is this surface static or floating?
2. Is a shadow communicating depth, or just decoration?
3. Does the treatment still work in dark mode?
4. Is state feedback handled by state styles instead of elevation?
5. Does this component use semantic surface tokens rather than primitive colors?

# Typography

The type system targets dense information interfaces rather than marketing pages. Body text starts at 15px—between compact 14px UI conventions and the browser's 16px default—to balance information density with sustained reading.

## Design intent

I wanted a scale that serves three very different surfaces from the same tokens: portfolio pages with expressive display type, documentation with dense readable prose, and app panels with compact controls. The solution is one responsive scale plus an independent `--typography-scale` multiplier that any subtree can adjust.

The shipped scale is deliberately not fluid. It uses viewport breakpoints for pages and `data-window-size` overrides for OS windows, so a constrained window can use its own size band even on a wide viewport. The separate `data-a63-type-scale` axis adjusts the whole ramp for user preference.

## Font families

| CSS variable | Tailwind | Stack |
|--------------|----------|-------|
| `--font-family-sans` | `font-sans` | Geist, system UI |
| `--font-family-serif` | `font-serif` | Brawler, Georgia |
| `--font-family-mono` | `font-mono` | Geist Mono, monospace |

I chose Geist because it's optimized for interfaces — generous x-height, clear at small sizes, and a mono companion that shares the same metrics. Brawler is reserved for rare editorial moments in the portfolio; the system defaults to sans everywhere.

## How the scale works

Thirteen steps from `xs` (12px) to `9xl` (39px at mobile, 49px at `768px+`). The scale grows at `640px` and `768px`, and `[data-window-size='xs'|'sm'|'md'|'lg'|'xl']` applies the same bands inside OS windows.

## Mental model

Typography has three separate jobs:

| Job | What it controls | Examples |
|-----|------------------|----------|
| Reading | Long-form comfort | Prose, docs, descriptions |
| Hierarchy | Relative importance | Page titles, section headers, labels |
| Density | How much interface fits | Sidebars, tables, controls, OS windows |

Do not solve all three with one heading scale. A docs page, a compact sidebar, and a portfolio hero need different hierarchy even when they share the same tokens.

### Line-height strategy

Body text (`xs` through `lg`) uses a ~1.5× ratio for comfortable reading. Display sizes (`xl` and above) compress to ~1.25× — tighter line-height at large sizes prevents headings from floating away from their content.

### The scale multiplier

`--typography-scale` defaults to `1`. The shipped `data-a63-type-scale` values map to `0.9` (`compact`), `1` (`normal`), `1.1` (`comfortable`), and `1.2` (`large`). OS window width is handled separately by `data-window-size`; the multiplier is a personalization control, not the window breakpoint mechanism.

## Decisions worth knowing

### 15px base, not 16px

Most systems use 16px because browsers default to it. I chose 15px after testing information-dense layouts — docs tables, prop references, sidebar navigation. At 16px, content felt loose and wasted space. At 14px, extended reading got fatiguing. 15px is the sweet spot for my use cases: dense enough for tool interfaces, comfortable enough for documentation prose.

### Breakpoints over fluid

Fluid typography (`clamp()`) assumes the viewport is the right proxy for text size. In the OS metaphor, multiple windows have arbitrary widths on one screen. Breakpoint jumps plus `data-window-size` attributes let window content follow its container band instead of the outer viewport.

### No heading-element-to-scale mapping in CSS

I don't automatically map `h1` to `9xl` or `h2` to `8xl` in the base tokens. Different surfaces need different heading scales — a docs `h2` should be smaller than a portfolio `h2`. The MDX variants handle heading sizing per context, and the raw scale stays available for explicit use via `text-*` utilities.

### Visual hierarchy and semantics are separate

A semantic `h2` does not always need to look like the second-largest text on the page. The `SectionHeader` pattern follows this rule: `variant` controls visual scale, while `level` can control document outline. That keeps accessibility and visual rhythm from fighting each other.

## Usage guidance

| Surface | Typical range | Scale multiplier |
|---------|---------------|------------------|
| Portfolio hero | `4xl`–`9xl` | Usually `normal`; user preference still applies |
| Documentation prose | `sm`–`xl` | `1` |
| App panels / OS windows | `xs`–`lg` | Window-size band + active type-scale axis |
| Code blocks | `sm` mono | `1` |

## Anti-patterns

```tsx
// Avoid: viewport-sized type inside a constrained panel.
```

The panel is narrow even if the viewport is wide. The text should respond to the container's role, not the browser width.

```tsx
// Prefer: choose a scale for the surface.
```

## Review checklist

When reviewing typography, ask:

1. Is this text sized for its container, not only the viewport?
2. Does the hierarchy still work if the content wraps?
3. Is the line-height comfortable for the amount of reading?
4. Are semantic heading levels valid independent of visual size?
5. Is display type reserved for display moments?

# Z-index

Stacking across windows and shell surfaces comes from one ordered scale of `--z-layer-*` tokens. Small numeric z-index values still exist inside isolated component stacking contexts; the shared scale governs layers that must compete across surfaces.

## Design intent

Z-index rots fast. The moment someone writes `z-[9999]` to win one fight, the next person writes `z-[99999]`, and soon nothing is predictable. I wanted a single ordered scale where every shell surface — windows, dock, menus, modals, overlays, the lock and boot screens — has exactly one home, and where adding a new surface means slotting it into a named order rather than inventing a number.

The scale is authored as CSS custom properties in `@atom63/styles` and mirrored to a typed `Z_LAYERS` object for JS consumers such as the OS63 windowing engine. CSS is the source of truth; the TypeScript mirror exists so runtime layout code can use named layers instead of raw numbers.

## How the scale works

The scale is banded. Each band answers a different question, which is why the numbers jump rather than increment evenly.

The bands matter more than the exact numbers:

- **In-context** layers (−1 to 90) only compete inside whatever element established the stacking context — a card, a window, the desktop canvas. Their values are small and reusable because they never escape their parent.
- The **window band** (300–399) is dynamic: focusing a window shuffles it within this range, and it compacts back down so windows never escape the ceiling.
- **Shell** and **System** layers (400+) are global. Notifications use the system `toast` layer at 1050, between the lock screen and boot screen. This is where the order has real consequences.

## Decisions worth knowing

### Portaled overlays live near the top, not at `z-50`

Menus, popovers, and tooltips render into a portal at `document.body`, so they stack against the whole app, not their trigger. A dropdown opened from the dock has to clear the dock. That is why `menu` (960), `popover` (970), and `tooltip` (980) sit above `dock` (900) instead of at the conventional `z-50`. The library default would have been correct only if these elements stayed inside their parent — they don't.

### Shell chrome outranks windows

The dock, menus, and tooltips all sit above the window band, which matches how both macOS and Windows behave: focusing a window restacks it only among other windows — it never lifts above the taskbar or a tooltip. Focus shuffling stays inside 300–399; nothing a window does pushes it past the shell.

### Task view and brightness are deliberate exceptions

The window overview (task view) is intentionally placed *above* the dock (905–940), because it is a full-shell mode whose scrim is meant to cover the dock. The brightness overlay sits at 990 — just under the lock screen — so dimming the display actually dims the chrome too, not just the desktop. Both were magic numbers before; tokenizing them kept the behavior while making the order legible.

### `below` exists for backplates

A few components paint an animated background *behind* their own content — the active-tab indicator, the segment-control backplate. Rather than scatter `-z-1`, there is one `below` (−1) token for "behind the local baseline."

## Usage guidance

| Surface | Token |
|---------|-------|
| Content lift, selected item | `base` |
| Sticky header inside a scroll area | `header` |
| A dialog / sheet | `modal` (with `scrim` behind) |
| A dropdown, select, or context menu | `menu` |
| A tooltip | `tooltip` |
| A full-screen system overlay | `overlay` |

Reach for a named Tailwind arbitrary value such as `z-[var(--z-layer-modal)]` in markup, or a named constant such as `Z_LAYERS.modal` from `@atom63/styles/z-layers` when the windowing engine needs the number.

## Anti-patterns

```tsx
// Avoid: a raw number to win a stacking fight.
```

```tsx
// Prefer: name the layer you actually mean.
```

Raw z-index for a new cross-surface layer in shared UI, OS63, or widgets should be treated as a review failure. Named CSS tokens and `Z_LAYERS` constants preserve the global stacking order. Local backplates and sibling anatomy may use small values when their stacking context is deliberately isolated.

## Review checklist

When reviewing stacking, ask:

1. Is the layer a named token, or a raw number that will rot?
2. Does the surface portal to `body`? If so, it belongs in the shell bands, not `z-50`.
3. Does a window try to outrank the dock, a menu, or a tooltip? It shouldn't.
4. If this is a new shell surface, does it slot into the existing order, or does it overlap an existing band?
5. For a backplate, is it using `below` rather than a fresh negative number?

# Atom63 Design System

Atom63 is an open-source design system with one token architecture behind every platform it ships to. The same tokens drive the React components, the SwiftUI components, and the Figma variables, so a decision made once reaches web, iOS, and design files without being restated.

## What ships

| Package | Platform | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@atom63/styles` | CSS | Tokens, themes, component contracts, and the token manifest every renderer reads |
| `@atom63/ui-foundation` | TypeScript | Platform-neutral component contracts and personalization axes |
| `@atom63/ui-react` | React | Components, layout, media, and theme controls |
| `Atom63UI` | SwiftUI | Native iOS components generated from the same tokens, distributed with Swift Package Manager |
| Figma plugin | Figma | Syncs the tokens into Figma variables, one collection per personalization axis |

2. **[Inspect the foundations](/foundations)** — color, type, surfaces, motion, and interaction, from raw values to semantic roles.

# Inform

`@atom63/inform` is the pattern for telling a visitor something or guiding them to a control. It has one message model, one arbiter that decides what shows, and four surfaces: a banner, a dialog, a corner flyout and a spotlight.

```bash
pnpm add @atom63/inform
```

```css
@import '@atom63/styles';
@import '@atom63/ui-react/recipes.css';
@import '@atom63/inform/styles.css';
```

The package ships its own stylesheet and needs no Tailwind. Every color, space, radius, shadow and duration reads an `--a63-*` token, so the surfaces follow the theme, brand, mode and density.

| Entry point | Contents |
|-------------|----------|
| `@atom63/inform` | Message types, `defineInformRegistry`, `resolveInform`, `createInformStore` and the dismissal stores. No React. |
| `@atom63/inform/react` | `InformProvider`, `InformOutlet`, `useInform`, `useInformContext`. |
| `@atom63/inform/surfaces` | The four surfaces, `InformFlyoutStack`, and the icon, media and dismiss slots. Controlled, usable without the runtime. |

## The message model

Messages are data in a registry, not call sites. Each one names the surface it uses, a severity, a priority, its content and how it is dismissed:

```tsx

  {
    id: 'maintenance',
    surface: 'banner',
    severity: 'warning',
    priority: 10,
    dismiss: 'session',
    endsAt: '2026-10-01T00:00:00Z',
    content: { title: 'Scheduled maintenance', body: 'Saving is paused from 02:00 to 03:00 UTC.' },
  },
  {
    id: 'command-menu',
    surface: 'spotlight',
    anchor: '#command-menu-trigger',
    severity: 'info',
    priority: 0,
    dismiss: 'persistent',
    when: ctx => ctx.pathname === '/',
    content: ctx => ({ title: 'Command menu', body: copy[ctx.locale].commandMenu }),
  },
])
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `id` | Stable identity and the dismissal key. `defineInformRegistry` rejects duplicates. |
| `surface` | `banner`, `dialog`, `corner-flyout` or `spotlight`. |
| `severity` | `info`, `success`, `warning` or `danger`. `info` is neutral; the others color the title and, on the banner, the border. |
| `priority` | Higher wins. Ties break by declaration order. |
| `dismiss` | `none` renders no dismiss control and never persists; `session` lasts until the tab closes; `persistent` survives it. |
| `version` | Bump it to show a message again to visitors who dismissed the previous revision. The dismissal key is `id:version`. |
| `startsAt`, `endsAt`, `when` | A time window and a predicate over the context (`pathname`, `locale`, `now`). |
| `anchor` | A CSS selector. Required on a spotlight and rejected on every other surface. |
| `content` | `title`, `body`, `actions`, and an optional `icon` and `media`, or a function of the context that returns them. Pass copy that is already localized. |

## The arbiter

`resolveInform` decides what each surface shows. It is a pure function of the registry, the context and the dismissals, so it is tested without a DOM:

1. **Filter.** A message drops out when it has been dismissed, is outside its time window, fails its `when` predicate, or is a spotlight whose anchor is not on the page.
2. **Rank** the rest per surface by priority, then declaration order.
3. **Exclude.** The dialog and the spotlight are blocking, and at most one of them shows; the dialog wins. While either is open the corner flyouts wait, and they come back when it closes. The banner is in the page flow and never takes part.
4. **Stack.** The banner, dialog and spotlight show one message each. The corner flyout shows up to three (`INFORM_FLYOUT_STACK_LIMIT`), and the rest queue until a visible card is dismissed.

The React layer wraps this in a store. Mount the provider once, and put outlets where the surfaces belong:

```tsx

```

The provider reads the dismissal storage after mount, never during render, so a dismissed message does not flash for a frame. Pass `dismissals={createMemoryDismissalStore()}` in tests and stories.

## The surfaces

Every surface is controlled: it renders what it is given and reports a dismissal through `onDismiss`. The outlet is one consumer of them; you can render any of them directly.

### Banner

An in-flow notice that scrolls away with the page. It announces itself as a polite `status` and never takes focus. Use it for a standing notice that concerns the whole page: maintenance, a beta warning, a policy change.

The leading icon and the dismiss control each sit in a slot exactly one line tall, so they line up with the first line of text whether the message is one line or four. The dismiss control keeps a 24px touch target without growing its box. A banner ignores `media`.

### Dialog

A blocking notice built on the ui-react `Dialog`, so focus trapping, Escape, scroll locking and background inerting come from the primitive. Use it when the visitor has to read something before continuing. It can show full-width `media` above the text, at a fixed aspect ratio so a late image load shifts nothing.

### Corner flyout

A persistent card in a screen corner. Unlike a toast it has an identity in the registry, holds rich content and actions, and waits to be dismissed instead of expiring. It announces itself as a polite `status` and never takes focus. Use the `toaster` for transient feedback about something the visitor just did; use a flyout for something they are meant to act on.

`InformFlyoutStack` places the cards in one corner (`placement`, `offset`). Collapsed, the front card shows in full and up to two peek out behind it; hovering or focusing the stack expands it. A card slides out before it reports its dismissal, and the next queued message takes its place. With `media`, the card shows a fixed square thumbnail in place of the severity icon, so its height stays predictable in the stack.

### Spotlight

A blocking guide step: a scrim with a cutout over one control and a bubble that explains it. The bubble flips above the control when there is no room below and stays inside the viewport. The spotlight traps focus, closes on Escape, restores focus on close and locks page scroll. Use it sparingly, for one control at a time; it is not a multi-step tour.

A spotlight whose anchor is missing or has no size is skipped, never drawn over nothing.

## Choosing a surface

| Situation | Surface |
|-----------|---------|
| Something about the whole page, safe to ignore for now | Banner |
| The visitor must read it before continuing | Dialog |
| Something to act on later, without interrupting | Corner flyout |
| Explaining one control where it sits | Spotlight |
| Feedback about an action the visitor just took | Not inform: use the `toaster` |

Severity must be carried by the words, not only the color or the icon: the icons are decorative and hidden from assistive technology.

# Page layout

`Page`, `Container`, and `Section` separate three decisions that otherwise drift together: the document landmark, the content frame, and the rhythm between page regions. They are composable defaults, not a required wrapper stack for every product shell.

## Responsibilities

| Primitive | Actual contract | Use when |
|-----------|-----------------|----------|
| `Page` | Renders `<main>`, fills the available height, and adds `pt-8 pb-20` unless `noPadding` is set | The route does not already have a main landmark |
| `Container` | Centers a named max-width, adds a fixed `gap-8` between direct children, and applies `p-6`, `px-6`, or no padding | Content needs a shared measure or inline inset |
| `Section` | Renders `<section>`, applies a spacing preset, and optionally spaces direct children | A real page region needs repeatable vertical rhythm |

`Container` padding is not responsive: `padding="all"` is `p-6`, while `padding="x"` is `px-6`. `Section` owns breakpoint-dependent vertical padding. `tight` stays `py-8`; `default` stays `py-16`; `loose` changes from `py-16` to `py-20` at 768px. `generous` progresses from `py-20` to `py-28` at 640px and `py-32` at 768px; `spacious` progresses from `py-24` to `py-32` and `py-40`. Its default `removeTopSpacing` is `true`, so a section keeps its bottom padding but removes only the top padding at every breakpoint; set it to `false` for an opening region that needs the preset on both sides.

## Default composition

```tsx

```

The first section opts into top spacing. The second uses the default top removal because the container gap and preceding section already establish separation.

## Shell-owned layout

Do not add wrappers only to match the diagram. Current consumers deliberately stop at different layers:

- Design-system and Learn routes render `Page noPadding` because their app shells own the outer frame, then use `Container` and `Section` for reading layout.
- atom63.io route screens commonly let `SiteShellLayout` own the route surface and compose `Container > Section` inside it.
- Full-bleed desktops, split panes, and other application shells should use their own layout rather than force a document-page pattern.


## Choose the layout owner

| Decision | Owner |
|----------|-------|
| Main landmark and route inset | `Page` or the app shell, never both |
| Maximum width and outer padding | `Container` |
| Space around a page region | `Section` |
| Gap between cards or controls | The local grid, stack, or component |
| Card padding and control internals | The component |

Nested containers are valid when a region intentionally changes measure. Otherwise they usually indicate that page and component spacing have been mixed together.

## Accessibility boundary

`Page` always renders `<main>`, so use it at most once in a document. `Section` always renders `<section>`; give the region an accessible heading rather than using it as a generic spacing wrapper. The primitives provide structure, but they do not infer a heading outline.

# Local layout

Page primitives own route measure and section rhythm. Local layout owns the relationship between children inside a toolbar, form, card body, list item, or collection.

Atom63 does not currently export `Stack`, `Inline`, `Cluster`, or `Split` components from `@atom63/ui-react`. These are composition names implemented with layout utilities. Naming the relationship is still useful; pretending there is a package API is not.

## Parent owns the relationship

Prefer a parent `gap` over child margins:

```tsx
// Avoid: the button carries placement that only makes sense here.
```

```tsx
// Prefer: the row owns the relationship.
```

This keeps each child portable and makes wrapping behavior visible where it is controlled.

## Choose the relationship

| Pattern | Composition | Use for |
|---------|-------------|---------|
| Stack | `flex flex-col` or `grid` + `gap` | Forms, settings groups, card bodies |
| Inline | `inline-flex` + `items-center` + `gap` | Icon-label pairs and fixed rows |
| Cluster | `flex flex-wrap` + `gap` | Tags, filters, responsive action sets |
| Split | `flex` + `justify-between` + `gap` | Title/action or label/value rows |
| Grid | `grid` + responsive columns + `gap` | Cards, galleries, comparison layouts |

```tsx

  ))}
```

```tsx

  ))}
```

Both shapes are present in current product code: action and filter sets wrap as clusters, while portfolio collections change column count at a breakpoint. The responsive decision belongs to the collection, not to `Container` or `Section`.

## Let components keep their contracts

Some components already own local arrangement:

- `Button` owns its icon, label, and loading-indicator layout.
- `ButtonGroup` owns adjacent control grouping.
- `InputGroup` owns addon and control placement.
- `SectionHeader` owns title and description rhythm.
- `Card` variants own their internal slots and padding.

Do not add outside margins to repair those internals. If the same variation is needed repeatedly, make it a supported component variant or compose a parent layout around the component.

## Spacing decisions

Use smaller gaps for tighter relationships:

| Relationship | Typical starting point |
|--------------|------------------------|
| Icon + label | `gap-1` or `gap-1.5` |
| Compact controls, tags | `gap-2` |
| Form rows, dense groups | `gap-3` |
| Standard card or panel flow | `gap-4` |
| Large local regions | `gap-6` |

These are starting points from the shared spacing scale, not a second token system. At `gap-8` and above, check whether the relationship is actually page rhythm and belongs to `Section`.

## Review rules

1. If spacing separates page regions, use `Section`.
2. If spacing is inside one reusable component, let the component own it.
3. If spacing is between composed children, let their parent own `gap`.
4. If wrapping changes reading or keyboard order, keep DOM order meaningful.
5. Promote a named primitive only after the same relationship and behavior recur across consumers.

# Section header

`SectionHeader` keeps visual hierarchy and document hierarchy separate. `variant` selects the type treatment; `level` selects the rendered heading element.

That distinction matters when a reusable region moves. A secondary-looking heading may be an `h2` on one route and an `h3` inside a nested section without changing its visual weight.

## The ramp

| Variant | Default element | Intended rank |
|---------|-----------------|---------------|
| `display` | `h1` | Rare editorial or route introduction |
| `primary` | `h1` | Main route or surface title |
| `secondary` | `h2` | Repeated page section |
| `muted` | `h3` | Supporting section |
| `subtle` | `h4` | Compact nested region |
| `label` | `p` | Category marker, not a section heading |

## Set semantics from context

```tsx
```

The stronger `primary` treatment does not force a second `h1`. Conversely, adding `level` to `label` turns the label into a real heading; do that only when it introduces a navigable region.

The component cannot inspect the rest of the page, so heading order remains the consumer's responsibility.

## Use the smallest sufficient variant

- Reserve `display` for a real top-level moment.
- Use `primary` for the main route title.
- Use `secondary` for most reusable sections.
- Use `muted` and `subtle` as hierarchy becomes denser.
- Use `label` for short categories, never as a visual substitute for an unlabeled section.

Current atom63.io design-system sections use `secondary` for repeated regions, while route introductions override the title classes for product-specific hero typography. That customization belongs to the consumer; it is not another shared ramp level.

Prefer changing `variant` before overriding `titleClassName` or `descriptionClassName`. Override classes only when a product surface has a deliberate type direction that the shared ramp should not absorb.

# Themes

Atom63 themes are CSS skins over one semantic system. They change material character without changing component anatomy, behavior, or product structure.

## The ownership boundary

I keep the layers separate so a skin can be expressive without becoming a second design system.

| Layer | Owns | Does not own |
|-------|------|--------------|
| Foundation | Shared palette, space, radius, type, blur, shadow, and motion dictionaries. | Aqua gel, Retro bevels, or Terminal phosphor recipes. |
| Semantics | Roles such as `--a63-surface-panel`, `--a63-text-secondary`, and `--a63-action-primary`. | Component anatomy or skin-specific stacks. |
| Contracts | Reusable family seams such as `--a63-control-shadow`, `--a63-field-shadow`, and `--a63-overlay-gloss`. | A new value dictionary for each component. |
| Themes | Contract assignments and skin-private material under `[data-a63-theme]`. Aqua and Terminal also make deliberate, mode-specific semantic paint overrides. | Slots, DOM, variants, accessibility, OS geometry, or app policy. |
| Recipes | Component structure, states, variants, and local CSS-variable mapping. | Per-theme branches. |

The canonical ownership rules live in `docs/design-system/authoring-surfaces.md`. When a theme needs a stop that another theme, a contract default, or an adapter also needs, that stop graduates into foundation.

## How the skin reaches UI

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  foundation["Foundation dictionaries"]
  semantics["Semantic roles"]
  contracts["Family contracts"]
  themes["Theme assignments"]
  recipes["Component recipes"]
  output["Rendered UI"]

  foundation --> semantics
  foundation --> contracts
  semantics --> contracts
  themes --> contracts
  themes -. "intentional paint overrides" .-> semantics
  contracts --> recipes
  semantics --> recipes
  recipes --> output
```

The contracts are deliberately broader than a component name. A skin can make raised controls glossy through `--a63-control-*`, or floating surfaces textured through `--a63-overlay-*`, without selecting every Button, Menu, or Dialog recipe.

## Shipped skins

| ID | Character | Current behavior |
|----|-----------|------------------|
| `modern` | Restrained identity baseline. | Explicit tactile control and field shadows, quiet segmented plates, and a subtle specialized-surface rim. |
| `aqua` | Translucent gel and specular depth. | Fixed blue surface cast, overlay-only pinstripes, blur, and separate light/dark paint. Primary actions still follow the brand axis. |
| `retro` | Early-web / Windows 98 tactility. | Hard bevel stacks, stronger borders, and collapsed press shadows while luminance inherits from mode semantics. |
| `terminal` | Monochrome CRT material. | Brand-derived phosphor glow, scanlines, control-level mono type, and separate light/dark surface and text paint. |

`modern` is not the absence of a theme. Its material values live under `[data-a63-theme='modern']`, so runtimes stamp it explicitly.

## Contract seams themes use

The current skins primarily assign:

- control material: `--a63-control-shadow`, `--a63-control-shadow-active`, `--a63-control-gloss`, `--a63-control-highlight`
- fields and tracks: `--a63-field-shadow`, `--a63-track-shadow`, with Terminal also assigning `--a63-field-background`
- surfaces and overlays: `--a63-surface-*` and `--a63-overlay-*` material handles for shadow, gloss, backdrop, border, and texture
- dense selection families: `--a63-segment-*`, `--a63-choice-*`, and `--a63-marker-*`
These are contract handles, not a promise that every handle is assigned by every skin. Recipe-local variables such as `--button-background` remain implementation details.

## What themes are not

Mode, brand, neutral surface, surface tint, radius, type scale, font, density, design language, input, OS, and icon presentation remain independent axes. A product may group them in one Appearance panel, but that UI grouping does not transfer ownership to the theme.

Old `[data-ui-theme]` and broad `--theme-*` component variables are archived migration residue. The live selector is `[data-a63-theme='<id>']`; slide themes use a separate `--theme-slide-*` contract.

Continue to [Theme system](/themes/theme-system) for selector rules, load order, runtime stamping, and the authoring workflow.

# Theme system

Theme authoring is a cascade problem: establish stable semantic and family contracts, then let one scoped skin assign material values. The difficult part is preserving that boundary as axes and products compose.

## IDs and selectors

`@atom63/ui-foundation` → `personalizationAxes.theme` is the authoritative value registry.

| ID | Selector | Source | Mode behavior |
|----|----------|--------|---------------|
| `modern` | `[data-a63-theme='modern']` | `themes/modern.css` | Inherits semantic light/dark paint; adds identity material. |
| `aqua` | `[data-a63-theme='aqua']` | `themes/aqua.css` | Adds material plus explicit light/dark surface paint. |
| `retro` | `[data-a63-theme='retro']` | `themes/retro.css` | Inherits semantic light/dark paint; adds bevel material. |
| `terminal` | `[data-a63-theme='terminal']` | `themes/terminal.css` | Reasserts explicit light/dark phosphor surfaces and text, including nested mode scopes. |

The old persisted ID `y2k` migrates to `retro`; it is not a selector or option. `[data-ui-theme]` is dead. OS63's `data-os63-ui-theme` is a temporary app-local bridge with the same IDs, not a second theme system.

## How axes compose

The axes are coordinates, not presets. Their ownership is intentionally uneven where a skin needs to establish a complete material:

| Axis | Owns | Theme interaction |
|------|------|-------------------|
| Mode | Luminance and base semantic paint. | Modern and Retro inherit it. Aqua and Terminal provide explicit light/dark skin paint. |
| Brand | Primary ramp and focus color. | Actions remain brand-driven. Terminal glow references `--a63-action-primary`; Aqua keeps its blue surface cast independent of the selected brand. |
| Surface + tint | Neutral family and its brand bend. | Modern and Retro receive the semantic result. Aqua and Terminal intentionally replace page/panel paint, so those surfaces do not receive the generic tint mix. |
| Radius | Multiplier across the shared radius ramp. | Themes may choose contract radius steps such as `var(--radius-sm)`; they do not replace the global radius axis with a hardcoded scale. |
| Font + type scale | Global type personality and scale. | Terminal adds mono styling to control contracts as skin character; the global font and scale still remain independently selectable. |
| Design language, input, density | Proportions, feedback, target size, and rhythm. | Themes do not own them. |
| OS | Caption controls, launcher geometry, and platform-conventional chrome paint. | It is a peer coordinate: `theme=aqua × os=windows` needs no new theme file. |
| Icon theme | React-rendered app-icon presentation. | It is not CSS theme material. |

This is why an Appearance panel can place several controls together without turning every combination into a named theme.

## CSS load order

The default `@atom63/styles` entry imports:

```text
tokens → contracts → themes → os → animations → utils
```

Contracts must precede themes because their root defaults and theme assignments can have the same specificity. Themes must win by source order. OS follows as a peer layer with separate `--a63-os-*` ownership; it should not compete for theme contract values.

Tailwind, compatibility aliases, and renderer recipes are opt-in consumer layers. Atom63 apps currently use this order:

```css
@import 'tailwindcss';
@import '@atom63/styles';
@import '@atom63/styles/tailwind';
@import '@atom63/styles/compat/shadcn';
@import '@atom63/ui-react/recipes.css';

@source '../../../../packages/ui-react/src/**/*.{ts,tsx}';
```

`@atom63/styles` already includes all four skins. Import a granular `@atom63/styles/themes/<id>` export only when building a deliberately partial bundle, not in addition to the default entry. `@source` registers Tailwind source files at build time; it is not a CSS cascade layer.

## Runtime stamping

There are four related APIs, and their names should not be treated as interchangeable:

| API | Responsibility |
|-----|----------------|
| `applyPersonalization(state, root?)` | Resolves `system` mode, stamps `.light` / `.dark`, mode, theme, brand, surface, type, radius, font, OS, and icon attributes, plus `--a63-surface-tint`. It always stamps `modern` explicitly. |
| `createPersonalizationController(...)` | Adds persisted state and optional wallpaper-derived auto-brand behavior around `applyPersonalization`. Existing product stores may implement the same `PersonalizationController` interface instead. |
| `UIProvider` | Creates a scoped subtree and stamps only supplied design-language, mode, theme, brand, input, density, and surface props. Unspecified axes inherit. Its local `mode='system'` path currently resolves to `light`; root system tracking belongs to the mode/personalization controller. |
| `createThemeProvider(...)` | Despite the legacy name, owns color mode only. It persists `light` / `dark` / `system` and writes the root mode class; it does not select a material theme or stamp `data-a63-theme`. |

`AppearancePanel` and `AppearanceMenu` are control surfaces over a controller. They do not own storage or theme CSS. The design-system app, atom63.io, and OS63 all adapt product state and then call the canonical stamper; OS63 additionally maintains bridge attributes for local variants.

## Private material

Theme files may keep scoped helpers and literal stacks that make sense only inside one skin. Current examples include `--aqua-overlay-drop`, `--retro-bevel-drop*`, and `--terminal-overlay-glow`, plus inline gel, bevel, and scanline recipes.

The boundary is reuse:

- keep a gel, bevel, CRT, or skin-only blur stack private while only that skin needs it
- promote a stop into foundation when a second theme, a contract default, or an adapter needs it
- continue assigning public `--a63-*` contracts from the private helper
- do not create a parallel component-facing namespace inside the theme

## Authoring and review workflow

1. Classify the change. A shared literal belongs in foundation; a role belongs in semantics; shared family physics may belong in a contract; skin material belongs in `themes/<id>.css`; product structure belongs outside Themes.
2. Reuse an existing family seam. Add a contract hook only when a second component or family needs it **and** a theme or design-language axis must override it.
3. Keep every selector under `[data-a63-theme='<id>']`. Add mode selectors only when the skin actually changes semantic paint.
4. If adding an ID, update the axis registry, UI option/type mirrors, theme index and package export, authoring harness, and only the product registries that support it.
5. Review both modes and representative brand, surface, radius, and OS coordinates. Storybook ThemeMatrix/contact sheets are manual craft review, not a CI screenshot gate.
6. Run `pnpm check:theme-authoring`. When contracts or recipes change, also run the affected `@atom63/styles` and `@atom63/ui-react` tests and `pnpm check:app-consumption`.

## Review decisions

Ask three questions:

1. Is this a **role**? Put it in semantics, such as `--a63-action-primary` or `--a63-surface-panel`.
2. Is this reusable **material physics**? Put the public seam in a family contract, such as `--a63-control-gloss` or `--a63-overlay-shadow`, and keep skin-private stacks in the theme.
3. Is this **product or platform behavior**? Put it in the app or OS layer. Theme CSS must not decide window controls, settings policy, wallpaper behavior, or which axes a product exposes.
